summary: This note describes the office of Governor-General of India, from its creation under the Regulating Act of 1773 through the British East India Company period, the Crown period after 1858, and its end on 26 January 1950. It covers the office's terms, the title changes at independence, and the summer relocation to Shimla. The note is a Wikipedia article with repeated infobox boilerplate that was ignored.
one_line: Overview of the Governor-General of India office, from its 1774 founding under Warren Hastings to its abolition in 1950.
key_facts: The first Governor-General of British India was Warren Hastings.
The first Governor-General of independent India was Louis Mountbatten.
The office of Governor-General of India was formed on 20 October 1774.
The office was abolished on 26 January 1950.
C. Rajagopalachari was the final holder of the office and the only Indian Governor-General.
The British government assumed partial control over governance of India through the Regulating Act of 1773, motivated by corruption in the East India Company.
Governors-General served at the pleasure of the sovereign, though the practice was to serve five-year terms.
Under the Regulating Act of 1773, a Governor-General and Supreme Council of Bengal were appointed to rule the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal.
The East India Company nominally acted as the agent of the Mughal Emperor when governing many parts of the Indian subcontinent.
Upon independence in August 1947, the title of Viceroy was abolished and the representative of the British Sovereign became known again as the Governor-General.
After independence, the Governor-General's role became almost entirely ceremonial, with power exercised day to day by the Indian cabinet.
After India became a republic in 1950, the President of India continued to perform the same functions.
Louis Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of India and the first Governor-General during the dominion period.
Throughout British administration, Governors-General retreated each summer to the Viceregal Lodge (Rashtrapati Niwas) at Shimla to escape the heat, and the government of India moved with them.
The Viceregal Lodge now houses the Indian Institute of Advanced Study.
